Lessons.Title: Fraction Games
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: use exact fraction multiplication and division to build the greatest or smallest possible product or quotient from permitted digits. This 2021 first-edition lesson focuses on reasoning about which number positions make an expression larger or smaller, not merely computing a fixed fraction answer.

Warm-up: estimate 28 multiplied by 2 8/9. Because 2 8/9 is between 2 and 3 and close to 3, the exact product is between 56 and 84, closer to 84. Convert 2 8/9 to 26/9 to verify 28 × 26/9 = 728/9 = 80 8/9. The estimate and justification use the source's mathematical structure; the worked wording here is first-party.

Activity 1 — build the greatest value: use different digits from 1 through 6 in the places allowed by the expression. For a whole number divided by a unit fraction, the quotient equals the whole number times the fraction's denominator. Try exchanges and argue that the two largest distinct digits give the greatest such product: 6 ÷ (1/5) = 30, or 5 ÷ (1/6) = 30. This is an independently authored illustration of the public preparation's optimization objective, not a transcription of a protected Cool-down.

Activity 2 — build the smallest value: for (1/a) ÷ b with distinct positive digits 1 through 6, the quotient is 1/(ab). Maximizing the product ab minimizes the positive quotient; the same largest distinct digits yield (1/6) ÷ 5 = 1/30, or (1/5) ÷ 6 = 1/30. Ask students to compare legal assignments and explain why exchanging a smaller chosen digit for an unused larger one improves the result.

Assessment boundary: numeric values and legal distinct-digit constraints can receive exact checks. Proving that a chosen expression is globally maximal or minimal, discussing alternate ties, and collaborating in the original partner activity require teacher review. Source: public IM K–5 Grade 5 Unit 3 Lesson 19 (2021) preparation. Publisher student PDF diagrams, Cool-down and any image artwork are not claimed reproduced or fully verified.

KeyConcepts.Title: Division by a unit fraction
KeyConcepts.Definition: Division asks how many unit-fraction groups fit in an amount.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For positive integers a,b, a ÷ (1/b) = a × b.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unit fraction divided by a whole number
KeyConcepts.Definition: The unit fraction is split into equal smaller parts.

KeyConcepts.Title: Maximum and minimum under constraints
KeyConcepts.Definition: An extreme value must respect every allowed digit and use restriction.
KeyConcepts.Rule: To maximize a×b with distinct digits 1–6 choose 6 and 5; to minimize 1/(ab), maximize the same positive denominator.

KeyConcepts.Title: Justifying the best choice
KeyConcepts.Definition: A good candidate is not enough without reasoning that no permitted alternative is better.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compare factors and show that replacing one selected digit by an unused larger digit increases a positive product.
KeyConcepts.Example: A legal pair (4,6) makes 24, less than (5,6) making 30.

WorkedExamples.Title: Largest whole ÷ unit fraction
WorkedExamples.Question: With distinct digits 1–6 in a ÷ (1/b), what is the greatest possible quotient?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the inverse relation a ÷ (1/b) = a × b, then optimize the product.
Steps: All candidates are products of two distinct positive digits up to six.
The two largest different digits are six and five.
Compute 6 ÷ (1/5) = 6 × 5 = 30 and give a reason smaller digits cannot exceed this.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both use distinct legal digits; any other pair has at least one factor smaller than 5 or 6.

WorkedExamples.Title: Smallest unit fraction ÷ whole
WorkedExamples.Question: With distinct digits 1–6 in (1/a) ÷ b, what is the least positive quotient?
WorkedExamples.Method: Convert the quotient to the reciprocal of a product and maximize its denominator.
Steps: The largest product of two distinct allowed digits is 6×5 = 30.
WorkedExamples.Check: For positive denominators, 1/30 is smaller than 1/k for every positive k under 30.

WorkedExamples.Title: Estimate a fractional product
WorkedExamples.Question: Estimate 28 × 2 8/9, then calculate exactly.
WorkedExamples.Method: Bound the mixed number between two whole numbers before multiplying.
Steps: The mixed number is close to 3, so expect a product a little smaller than 84.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 80 8/9; an estimate of roughly 81 is sensible.
WorkedExamples.Check: 80 8/9 is between 56 and 84 and close to 84, as expected.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Division always makes the number smaller
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Dividing a whole number by a unit fraction such as 1/5 counts many small groups.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use 6 ÷ (1/5) = 30 to check which interpretation the question uses.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: A large-looking fraction automatically makes the best expression
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Changing a numerator or denominator has a different effect depending on whether the fraction is the divisor or dividend.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Rewrite the exact expression as a product or reciprocal, then compare legal digit assignments.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: A correct extreme value is a complete argument
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Finding 30 or 1/30 does not, by itself, establish that no other permitted choice is better.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Explain why the two largest distinct legal digits give the greatest positive product.

SummaryPoints: For positive integers a,b, a ÷ (1/b) = ab while (1/a) ÷ b = 1/(ab); changing the order changes the result.
Optimize under the exact legal digit rules, verify the arithmetic and justify why no other assignment can improve the result.
The written optimality explanation, alternate ties and peer game are teacher-reviewed even when a supporting numeric answer can be checked.
